newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers fail to agree on gas liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers fail to agree on gas liberalisation.

text.p: European Union energy ministers failed on Tuesday to find a formula for the liberalisation of the EU gas market but the Dutch chairman of the Energy Council said he still hoped he could broker a deal next month.

The Dutch, who hold the EU presidency until June 30, had proposed a compromise on the three major obstacles to a deal on liberalisation -- how to structure market opening, how to treat long term take-or-pay contracts and what exemptions from competition rules to allow emerging markets and regions.
But while ministers succeeded in narrowing their differences, too many difficulties remained for an agreement on any of these crucial issues.

Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers told a news conference after the meeting he would consult individual EU states during the week before deciding whether there was enough convergence of views to try for a ministerial accord on June 24.
Chances of a deal before Luxembourg took over the EU presidency on July 1 were "fifty-fifty", he said.
EU officials said a consensus appeared to be emerging around a two-tier formula for progressively liberalising national gas markets although no one is prepared yet to talk figures.

The formula allows certain "eligible customers" -- electricity generators and large industrial customers who consume more that a set amount of gas a year -- to negotiate contracts directly with the gas supplier of their choice.
It also sets an obligatory minimum level of liberalisation and an optional maximum ceiling.

EU Energy Commissioner Christos Papoutsis insisted at the meeting that over the next 10 years the consumption threshold should be lowered to increase the numbers of eligible customers while the minimum and maximum percentages of market opening should be increased.

But a deal will only be possible if the Commissioner can overcome the reticence of the French, who want the minimum- maximum percentages to remain unchanged, and other member states led by the Dutch, who do not want to alter the threshold for eligible customers.

Divisions also remain about who will be responsible for authorising restrictions on market access for new suppliers in cases where introducing competition would cause a crisis for distributors locked into long term take-or-pay contracts with suppliers in Russia, Algeria and Norway.
The Commission insists the final say on future take-or-pay contracts should rest with the EU authorities in Brussels, a view backed by the Dutch, the British, the Danish and the Finns.
But other member states, particularly Germany, are arguing strongly for power to remain with national authorities.
Whatever the outcome, ministers will still have to set strict rules for allowing derogations.

Ministers did manage to agree in principle that the emerging Portuguese and Greek gas markets should be given temporary derogations from competition rules but there was no accord on emerging regions in other member states.
Over the next few weeks, national governments will be asked to submit to the Commission a list of isolated or undeveloped regions for which they want derogations.
In the meantime, Commisison officials will endeavour to draw up strict eligibility criteria. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
